title: Teaching university courses in English

turns.speaker: Noor
turns.text: Two thirds of the master's programmes here are taught in English now, in a country where that isn't the language.

turns.speaker: Hakim
turns.text: Which brings in international students and the fees that come with them.

turns.speaker: Ilse
turns.text: And makes the research readable by everyone, which genuinely matters in a small language.

turns.speaker: Noor
turns.text: The cost is that the subject stops existing in the local language. Nobody's writing new terminology for it.

turns.speaker: Ilse
turns.text: That's the long-term worry. A language that can't discuss immunology in its own words has lost something it won't get back easily.

turns.speaker: Hakim
turns.text: Is there evidence about the learning itself?

turns.speaker: Noor
turns.text: There is, and it's mixed. Students in a second language ask fewer questions and take worse notes, at least early on.

turns.speaker: Ilse
turns.text: And the lecturer is often in their second language too, which nobody mentions.

turns.speaker: Hakim
turns.text: That's the part I'd fix first. A brilliant researcher teaching badly in English is worse than teaching well in anything.

turns.speaker: Noor
turns.text: The Dutch pushed back on this and capped the proportion, largely on access grounds rather than culture.

turns.speaker: Ilse
turns.text: Because local students were being priced and taught out of their own universities.

turns.speaker: Hakim
turns.text: A split seems reasonable. Undergraduate in the local language, postgraduate in English.

turns.speaker: Noor
turns.text: Which is roughly where most systems end up after arguing about it for a decade.

points: Two thirds of master's programmes are taught in English in a non-English-speaking country, attracting international fees.
Ilse notes the benefit of research being widely readable, important for a small language.
The cost is that academic subjects cease to exist in the local language, with no new terminology being developed.
Evidence on learning is mixed, with second-language students asking fewer questions and taking poorer notes early on.
Lecturers are often also working in a second language, which Hakim would address first.
The Dutch capped English-taught provision on access grounds, and they conclude a split between local-language undergraduate and English postgraduate teaching is the common outcome.
